960.title: Exile in Burma
960.hook: Baba Ram Singh was exiled to Rangoon
960.howItsDone: Namdhari Sikhs remember Baba Ram Singh's exile to Burma, keep letters they hold he wrote from there, and Namdhari tradition looks for his return.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Malerkotla, and your line was remembered. Whose name did you say? Today, what happened to the teacher himself. Day nine hundred sixty.

A ship pulls away from the coast of India, heading east across the Bay of Bengal. On board, under guard, is a man in white who has never been tried for any crime. He's being taken to Rangoon, in Burma, a country where he doesn't speak the language, far from his village, his people and the fields of the Punjab. The British have decided to keep Baba Ram Singh far from anyone who might gather around him. Today: exile in Burma.
screen: `A SHIP HEADING EAST.` → `A MAN IN WHITE, UNDER GUARD.` → `NEVER TRIED.` → `RANGOON, FAR FROM THE PUNJAB.`

segments.voice: First, the arrest. After Malerkotla, the British took Baba Ram Singh into custody, even though, as you heard yesterday, Namdhari histories say he hadn't sent the raiders. He wasn't put on trial. Instead, the government used an old regulation that let it hold a person as a state prisoner without charges, and sent him far from the Punjab, across the sea. Second, the place. Burma was then ruled from British India, and Rangoon was its port city. For a teacher whose whole life was a village, a congregation and the sound of the Name recited together, this was very far from home. He was kept under watch, with few of his own people allowed near. Third, the letters. Namdharis keep letters said to have been written by Baba Ram Singh in exile and carried back to the Punjab. In them, the community remembers, he encouraged his followers to hold to the Name and to their discipline. Exile cut the road, but not every thread. Fourth, how the story ends, and who says what. British records say he died in Burma. Namdhari tradition holds that he did not die there, and looks for his return. That belief belongs to the Namdhari community, and this lesson simply reports it. Punjabi has a word for the one far from home: pardesi, the traveler in a strange land. Some readers of the Guru's hymns hear the soul itself pictured that way, a guest in this world, longing for home. Baba Ram Singh lived that picture in his body.
screen: `HELD WITHOUT TRIAL.` · `RANGOON, A PORT FAR EAST.` · `LETTERS CARRIED HOME.` · `WHO SAYS WHAT ABOUT THE END.` · then, large: `FAR FROM HOME.`

segments.voice: Two minutes for the exiled. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind someone who lives far from home, not by choice: a refugee, a prisoner, a person sent away, someone who can't go back. You don't need to know their name. Picture them waking up somewhere strange today. On each breath out, wish them one thing: safety, or a letter from home, or a familiar voice. If you pray, you can hold them before Waheguru in the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Exile in Burma. Baba Ram Singh, held without trial, sent to Rangoon, and remembered by his followers through the letters they say he sent home. Today's word.
Your line: far from home. Today, if someone near you comes from far away, ask them one thing about home, and listen to the answer. Day nine hundred sixty.

961.title: Amritsar's Singh Sabha, 1873
961.hook: Sikhs in Amritsar formed a society to renew teaching, schools and literature
961.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Singh Sabha of Amritsar as the start of a renewal of Sikh teaching, schools and Punjabi books; study circles and gurdwara classes carry on that work today.

segments.voice: Yesterday, exile in Burma, and your line was far from home. Who did you reach out to? Today, back in the Punjab, people start to gather. Day nine hundred sixty-one.

A room in Amritsar. A group of Sikh gentlemen sit together, worried. The kingdom is gone. The old schools are thin. Printed books in Punjabi are hard to find. And news has come that some Sikh students at a mission school plan to leave the faith. Nobody in the room has an army. What they have is a meeting. And by the end of it, they've founded a society with a plain name. Today: Singh Sabha.
screen: `A ROOM IN AMRITSAR.` → `THE KINGDOM IS GONE.` → `NO ARMY, ONLY A MEETING.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Singh, the lion, is the name Khalsa men take. Sabha means an assembly or society. So Singh Sabha is simply the society of the Singhs, a gathering of Sikhs with a purpose. Second, the worry. After the loss of the kingdom, Sikh leaders saw learning slipping away. Histories say the spark included word that a few Sikh students at a Christian mission school were about to be baptized. Christian missionaries, as you heard some days ago, were active in the Punjab and debated in the open. The founders' answer, as the histories tell it, was to turn inward: to teach their own young people their own Gurus. Third, what they set out to do. Renew Sikh teaching as the Gurus gave it. Open schools. Print books and papers in Punjabi, in the Gurmukhi letters. Welcome back those who had drifted away. And, under British rule, they sought the goodwill of officials for their schools. Fourth, why a meeting matters. Guru Nanak asks, in a hymn in Sri Rag, how the true congregation is recognized, and answers that it's the place where the One Name is spoken. The Singh Sabha was a congregation for a new age: not a court or a camp, but people sitting together to study and teach. In the years that followed, other Singh Sabhas sprang up in other towns, and tomorrow you'll meet a bolder one. Renewal, here, begins in a room with a few chairs.
screen: `SINGH SABHA — SOCIETY OF THE SINGHS.` · `LEARNING SLIPPING AWAY.` · `SCHOOLS, BOOKS AND PUNJABI.` · `WHERE THE ONE NAME IS SPOKEN.` · then, large: `RENEWAL BEGINS.`

segments.voice: Two minutes to plan a small gathering. Sit, and breathe slowly. Think of two or three people who might like to learn something with you: a text, a skill, a question you share. Picture the place: a kitchen table, a call, a corner of a library. Picture the first ten minutes: one reads, the others listen, someone asks a question. Don't solve the details. Just see it. If you pray, you can ask in your own words for a good sangat, the company of seekers. The bell holds the time.
Singh Sabha. The society of the Singhs, formed in Amritsar to renew Sikh teaching, schools and books. Today's word.
Your line: renewal begins. Today, start a small study group, or send the first message that could start one. Day nine hundred sixty-one.

962.title: The Lahore Sabha, 1879
962.hook: a bolder reform society formed in Lahore
962.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Lahore Singh Sabha for its plain insistence, in Punjabi papers and pamphlets, that all Sikhs stand equal before the Guru whatever their birth.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Singh Sabha in Amritsar, and your line was renewal begins. Did you send the first message? Today, a second Sabha, in a second city, with a sharper voice. Day nine hundred sixty-two.

Lahore, the old capital of Ranjit Singh's kingdom, is now a British city of colleges, printing presses and newspapers. A young teacher at a college there, and a circle of friends around him, have been watching the Amritsar Sabha. They agree with its aims. But they think it's too polite. Too careful with old privileges. Too slow to say plainly what the Gurus said. So they start their own. Today: the Lahore Sabha.
screen: `LAHORE, A CITY OF PRESSES.` → `A YOUNG TEACHER AND HIS FRIENDS.` → `TOO POLITE, TOO SLOW.`

segments.voice: First, who they were. The Lahore Singh Sabha gathered teachers, clerks and writers, people who lived by books and print. Professor Gurmukh Singh was among its leaders, and Giani Ditt Singh, a writer you'll meet tomorrow, joined it. Second, what they said out loud. All Sikhs are equal before the Guru, whatever family they were born into. No one is owed special honor in the sangat because he descends from a Guru's family. Caste has no place at the Guru's door. In a hymn in Sri Rag, Guru Nanak says he stands with the lowest of the low, and has no wish to vie with the great. The Lahore reformers took that line at its word. Third, the clash. The Amritsar leaders included men of honored lineages, some descended from the Gurus' own families, who held that old customs and old respect deserved a place. The Lahore group thought this blurred the Gurus' teaching. The two Sabhas formed rival councils, and their disagreement was public and sometimes bitter. Each side believed it was protecting the Panth. Historians still weigh both sides, and this lesson leaves the judging to them. Fourth, the tool. The Lahore reformers spoke clearly in print: papers and pamphlets in Punjabi, passed from hand to hand. A sentence on a page could travel further than a speech in a hall. Speaking clearly isn't the same as shouting. It means saying the thing plainly, so nobody has to guess what you meant.
screen: `TEACHERS, CLERKS AND WRITERS.` · `ALL EQUAL BEFORE THE GURU.` · `TWO SABHAS, TWO COUNCILS.` · `SPEAKING CLEARLY IN PRINT.` · then, large: `SPEAK CLEARLY.`

segments.voice: Two minutes to find one clear sentence. Sit, and breathe slowly. Think of something that matters to you that you've been saying in a roundabout way, or not at all. A need, a thanks, a boundary. Let the extra words fall off, one by one, until there's a single plain sentence left. Hold that sentence and breathe with it. It doesn't need to be sharp. Just clear. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between the breaths. The bell holds the time.
The Lahore Sabha. The bolder Singh Sabha, which said plainly in print that all Sikhs stand equal before the Guru. Today's word.
Your line: speak clearly. Today, say the one sentence you found, plainly and kindly, to the person who needs to hear it. Day nine hundred sixty-two.

963.title: Giani Ditt Singh
963.hook: a scholar from a family counted low became a leading Sikh writer
963.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Giani Ditt Singh as a writer and editor of the Singh Sabha reform who rose from a family counted low, and the title Giani is still given to those learned in the Gurus' word.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lahore Sabha, and your line was speak clearly. Did you say your one plain sentence? Today, one of the clearest voices that Sabha had. Day nine hundred sixty-three.

In a Punjab village, a boy is born into a family the caste order counts low. People like him are expected to work with their hands, keep their eyes down, and leave books to others. This boy doesn't. He learns to read. He learns poetry and argument. He studies with one religious teacher after another, asking hard questions. And one day, in Lahore, he's editing a Sikh newspaper in Punjabi. He's called Giani, the learned one. Today: Giani Ditt Singh.
screen: `A FAMILY COUNTED LOW.` → `A BOY WHO LEARNS TO READ.` → `EDITING A SIKH NEWSPAPER.`

segments.voice: First, the title. Giani means a learned one. In Sikh life it's a title for a person learned in the Gurus' word and able to explain it. Nobody is born a Giani. It's earned with years of study. Second, the search. Before he took the Khalsa's amrit, Ditt Singh moved through more than one religious circle, listening, reading, testing. When he came to the Gurus' path, he came as a thinker who had looked around, not as someone who'd never been asked. Third, the work. In Lahore he joined the Singh Sabha you met yesterday and became one of its sharpest writers. He edited the Khalsa Akhbar, a Punjabi paper of the reform, and wrote books and pamphlets in plain Punjabi: stories, verse, and arguments about what the Gurus taught. Tradition remembers him in public debate too. Fourth, why his birth matters to the story. Guru Nanak says, in a hymn in Asa, to recognize the divine light in each person and not to ask about their caste, because caste counts for nothing hereafter. The Lahore reformers said all Sikhs are equal before the Guru. Ditt Singh's own life put that teaching in plain view. Men of honored lineage sometimes sneered at his birth, and he answered them with his pen. In the Sikh tradition, his story says, learning isn't a family inheritance. It's open to anyone who sits down and does the work.
screen: `GIANI — A LEARNED ONE.` · `A SEEKER WHO LOOKED AROUND.` · `EDITOR AND WRITER IN LAHORE.` · `DON'T ASK ABOUT CASTE.` · then, large: `LEARNING FOR ALL.`

segments.voice: Two minutes to honor a self-made scholar. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind someone who taught themselves, or who learned against the odds: a grandparent who read late at night, a coworker who studied after shifts, a writer whose story you know. Picture them at the table with the book open. Breathe in, and name one thing they learned. Breathe out, and wish them well, wherever they are. If you pray, you can hold them before Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Giani Ditt Singh. Born into a family counted low, he became a Giani, a learned one, and a leading writer and editor of the Sikh reform. Today's word.
Your line: learning for all. Today, thank or honor one person who earned their learning the hard way, out loud if you can. Day nine hundred sixty-three.

964.title: Professor Gurmukh Singh
964.hook: a teacher who pushed for Punjabi and Sikh education
964.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Professor Gurmukh Singh as a Lahore teacher and Singh Sabha leader who pushed for Punjabi in Gurmukhi and for Sikh education, and whose excommunication the Akal Takht later declared void.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Giani Ditt Singh, and your line was learning for all. Who did you honor for the learning they earned? Today, the friend who stood beside him. Day nine hundred sixty-four.

A classroom in Lahore. Chalk on the board. The students are learning in a city where the language of government is English, the language of the courts is Urdu, and the language of their own homes, Punjabi, barely has a place in school. Their teacher thinks that's a problem worth spending his life on. If Sikh children can't read Punjabi in the Gurmukhi letters, how will they read the Guru's word? He's a professor and a reformer, and his reforms will cost him. Today: Professor Gurmukh Singh.
screen: `A CLASSROOM IN LAHORE.` → `PUNJABI HAS BARELY A PLACE.` → `HOW WILL THEY READ THE GURU'S WORD?`

segments.voice: First, the classroom. Gurmukh Singh taught at Oriental College in Lahore, and he pressed for Punjabi to be taught properly, in Gurmukhi, the script of the Guru Granth Sahib. A language that isn't taught in school slowly becomes a language only for the kitchen. He wanted it in the classroom. Second, the organizer. He was among the leaders of the Lahore Singh Sabha you met two days ago, and he worked to link the Singh Sabhas into a wider council. He started papers, gathered writers like Giani Ditt Singh, and argued for a Sikh college where young Sikhs could study modern subjects without losing their own tradition. Third, the price. His plain teaching on equality angered powerful men in Amritsar, including some of honored lineage. Priests there issued an edict casting him out of the Panth. He kept teaching anyway. Much later, the Akal Takht itself declared that edict void, restoring his name. The record was corrected, long after the man was gone. Fourth, what a teacher is in the Sikh tradition. The word Sikh, Sikh teachers explain, means a learner, a disciple. And the Gurus are teachers. The Guru's hymns speak of the true Guru as the one who joins the seeker to the Name. A human teacher isn't the Guru, but a good one points the way. Gurmukh Singh spent his life pointing young people toward their own language and their own scripture. Everyone knows something worth passing on. A teacher is just someone who stops to pass it.
screen: `PUNJABI IN THE CLASSROOM.` · `LINKING THE SABHAS.` · `CAST OUT, LATER RESTORED.` · `SIKH MEANS A LEARNER.` · then, large: `THE TEACHER.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with something you know. Sit, and let your breath settle. Think of one thing you know how to do well: a recipe, a shortcut, a song, a way of calming down, a few words of another language. Now think of one person who might want to know it. Picture yourself showing them, slowly, the way a good teacher would, without hurry, without making them feel small. Breathe with that picture. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between the breaths. The bell holds the time.
Professor Gurmukh Singh. A Lahore teacher who pushed for Punjabi and Sikh education, was cast out by an edict, and was later restored by the Akal Takht. Today's word.
Your line: the teacher. Today, teach one thing you know to one person, slowly and kindly. Day nine hundred sixty-four.

965.title: Khalsa College, 1892
965.hook: a Sikh college rises in Amritsar
965.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Khalsa College in Amritsar as a fruit of the Singh Sabha reform, built with gifts from Sikh princes and ordinary Sikhs, and it still teaches students today.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Professor Gurmukh Singh, and your line was the teacher. What did you teach, and to whom? Today, the college he argued for. Day nine hundred sixty-five.

Outside Amritsar, on open ground along the road toward Lahore, a crowd gathers for a foundation stone. British officials in formal dress. Supporters from the Sikh princely states. Singh Sabha reformers, teachers and writers. And ordinary Sikhs who've given what they could, so that this could happen. Nothing stands there yet but a stone and a plan. The plan is a college where young Sikhs can learn science and English without being taught to leave their Gurus behind. Today: Khalsa College.
screen: `A FOUNDATION STONE.` → `PRINCES, REFORMERS, ORDINARY GIVERS.` → `A COLLEGE NOT YET BUILT.`

segments.voice: First, why a college. The Singh Sabha reformers had schools and papers. But young Sikhs who wanted higher study went to colleges run by the government or by missions, and some, as the reformers saw it, came back strangers to their own tradition. The reformers wanted a place that taught the modern subjects and Sikh learning under one roof. Second, who paid. Sikh rulers of the princely states gave large sums. The British government gave its support. And collections went around the Punjab, in towns and villages, from people with little to spare. The college belonged, in that sense, to everyone who put something in. Third, the name. Khalsa is the name Guru Gobind Singh gave the community of the initiated, those who belong directly to the Guru. A Khalsa College says what it's for in its name: a college for that community, open to learning from anywhere, rooted in the Guru's word. Over time, a great building rose on that ground, and generations of students passed through it. Fourth, what the Gurus say about learning. In a hymn in Asa, Guru Nanak says that when learning is truly reflected on, the learned one becomes a help to others. Learning that stays in the head, or serves only pride, misses the point. The founders hoped the college would turn out graduates who served: teachers, doctors, writers and leaders who carried what they'd learned back into the Panth. A college is, in the end, a promise that learning will be passed on. Every time you learn something new and share it, you keep a small version of that promise.
screen: `WHY A SIKH COLLEGE.` · `PRINCES, OFFICIALS, ORDINARY GIVERS.` · `KHALSA — THE GURU'S OWN.` · `LEARNING THAT HELPS OTHERS.` · then, large: `A COLLEGE FOR THE KHALSA.`

segments.voice: Two minutes for something new. Sit, and breathe slowly. Choose one small thing you'd like to learn this week: a word of Punjabi, a line of a hymn, how a plant grows, the name of a street you walk down. Hold it in mind as a question. Breathe in, curious. Breathe out, patient. Then ask one more thing: who could this help, once I know it? Let that person come to mind. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between the breaths. The bell holds the time.
Khalsa College. The Sikh college founded in Amritsar to teach modern subjects alongside the Gurus' learning, built with gifts from princes and ordinary Sikhs. Today's word.

966.title: We are not Hindus
966.hook: Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's book argued Sikhi was distinct, while honoring neighbors
966.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's Ham Hindu Nahin as a scholar's case, built from the Gurus' hymns, that Sikhi is a distinct path, written with respect for Hindu neighbors.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Khalsa College, and your line was a college for the khalsa. What did you learn and pass on? This week ran from exile in Burma through the Sabhas, Ditt Singh, Gurmukh Singh and a college. It ends with a book. Day nine hundred sixty-six.

A book title can sound like a slammed door. This one, in Punjabi, is Ham Hindu Nahin: we are not Hindus. Read only the cover and you might expect an attack. Open it, and the author starts somewhere else. He's writing to his Hindu neighbors and friends with respect, he says, and he means them no ill will. He simply wants to set down, plainly, from the Gurus' own words, what makes the Sikh path its own. The author is Bhai Kahn Singh of Nabha. Today: we are not Hindus.
screen: `A TITLE LIKE A SLAMMED DOOR.` → `OPEN IT: RESPECT FIRST.` → `BHAI KAHN SINGH OF NABHA.`

segments.voice: First, the question. In the years of the Singh Sabhas, a debate ran through the Punjab: were Sikhs a separate faith, or a branch of the wider Hindu family? Some Hindu reformers held that Sikhs belonged within the Hindu fold, and some Sikhs agreed. Other Sikhs disagreed sharply. Feelings ran high on every side. Second, the scholar. Kahn Singh was a learned man from the princely state of Nabha, at home in Punjabi, Persian and the old texts. He answered the question the way a scholar does: not with insults, but with quotations. Page after page, he set the Gurus' hymns beside the claim, and let the hymns speak. Third, his evidence. The Sikhs, he argued, have their own Guru, the Guru Granth Sahib; their own initiation, the Khalsa's amrit; their own rites for birth, marriage and death; their own places of worship. And he pointed to the Gurus themselves, including the hymn you met at the family table some days ago: Guru Arjan, in Bhairo, saying he is neither Hindu nor Muslim, and that his body and breath belong to the One whom some call Allah and some call Ram. Kahn Singh read it as the Gurus marking out a path of their own. Fourth, the kindness. In the Punjab, some Sikh and Hindu families were kin, sharing weddings, festivals and grief. Kahn Singh's book draws a line around the Sikh path, but it doesn't push the neighbors away. That balance is today's line. Hindus, of course, describe their own traditions in their own words, and this lesson isn't the place to describe them. It's about how one Sikh scholar said who his community was. His book is one picture of saying clearly who you are while still sitting at a neighbor's table.

segments.voice: Two minutes for saying who you are. Sit, and let your breath slow. Finish this sentence quietly, in your own words: I am someone who… Let one honest answer come: a faith, a practice, a value, a place you belong. Now picture saying it to a neighbor who sees the world differently. Say it again in your head, with the same words, but warmer. Notice that the truth didn't change, only the tone. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between the breaths. The bell holds the time.
